thread.title: Volatility Has Returned! Wait, What Is Volatility Again?

author: SA Editor Mike Taylor, CFA
title: Volatility Has Returned! Wait, What Is Volatility Again?
text:
Dear ESSENTIAL subscribers:
Hi! I'm Seeking Alpha managing editor Mike Taylor. Welcome to ESSENTIAL Weekly, a subscriber-exclusive look at Seeking Alpha's top news and analysis. I'll guide you through this week's market themes, highlight some analysis you might have missed, and preview coming attractions for SA subscribers.
Don't be bashful: We need to hear from you so we can make ESSENTIAL the best investment research tool available anywhere. Let me know what the Seeking Alpha team can do - your feedback is key to our success.
Now let's get to the good stuff.
Volatility: The Salsa Of Investing I believe the same thing about volatility that Jerry Seinfeld believes about salsa . If the word didn't sound so cool, people wouldn't say it all the time.
George: Salsa is now the number one condiment in America.
Jerry: Do you know why? Because people like to say "salsa." Excuse me, do you have any salsa? We need more salsa! Where is the salsa? No salsa!
Volatility is popular because people like to say "volatility." It starts with a "V," has a good trochaic meter, and it's menacing. Even though everyone knows volatility is bad, it's hard to say exactly what it is. It has some mystique.
Excuse me, do the markets have any volatility? We need more volatility! And for a lot of 2017: Where is the volatility? No volatility!
( Source: FRED )
Try replacing volatility with its truest analog: "Investors need to get ready for a possible surge in market... standard deviation ." Doesn't have the same ring to it, right?
But that's what volatility is, just a standardized range of outcomes distributed around expected returns. Thanks in large part to Harry Markowitz, most investors take standard deviation as a measure of risk. The bigger the range of outcomes, the more risk. (See note below)* Now all we need is a single catchy brand name to go with it. Voila. Volatility .
I've been hearing out in the streets that there's a renewed interest among asset managers and their clients in volatility. That probably owes to the increase we saw toward the end of December, as stocks got hammered to close 2018.
SPY data by YCharts
Fun as the word is to say, I don't think investors strictly care about volatility of stock prices/returns. But I do think volatility is connected with things investors do care about.
Investors care when stocks go down, especially when they go down a lot. Stocks have positive expected returns, so when stocks go down, their realized standard deviation is likely to be higher (to go negative, the returns have to vary from the expected value). To the extent that stock prices mirror fundamentals, a higher standard deviation of earnings results is the realization of greater volatility in business activities, and investors do prefer steadier returns vs. ones with greater variance. Volatility unexpectedly spikes, then calms down, giving it a special "bogey man" quality that goes well with its evil name and abstract definition. Questionable, but I'm including it: Do stocks go down faster than they go up? If so, investors would care about volatility inasmuch as they care about drawdowns. For more on this, check this very interesting article by Force Majeure. Now is when someone might give the "healthy correction"/"this is normal" talk. I'm a CAPE guy when it comes to broad stock market valuations, which means I don't think stocks are all that cheap right now. I'd be more interested in stocks from the long side if we had a few more December-like volatility spikes. (All opinions in this newsletter are my own, not those of Seeking Alpha.)
(Source: Barclays )
But more than that it's just a generational/cultural thing. I like volatility. I find it comforting.
I started covering the stock market in 2008 when the VIX spent considerable time above 50. The return of intraday volatility in late December feels more normal to me than the action of the past few years. It was weird when the major indices would pick a direction at the beginning of the day and then just hold there until the close. Stocks should put in a full day's work bouncing up and down, I say.
I'm not alone in the Seeking Alpha community on this point. Here's John Cochrane :
Twenty percent volatility is normal. Twenty percent volatility on top of a 5 percent average return means that every other year is likely to see a 15 percent drop.
And D.M. Martins Research :
The harsh reality is that volatility is a normal feature in market corrections. [...] Rather than looking at the recent spike as a sign that the bear market may be coming to an end, I believe it's much more indicative that the path forward is likely to remain bumpy and adrenaline filled.
Relevant disclosure: I've allocated a portion of my active portfolio to the PSQ ETF, which is short the Nasdaq.
Related: For a daily exploration of volatility and all its facets, readers should check out SA author The Balance of Trade . Also check out " Everybody's Doing It: Short Volatility Strategies and Shadow Financial Insurers " from the Financial Analysts Journal (abstract only).
*Yes, Michael Burry and Warren Buffett think standard deviation is a dumb risk metric, and they are very smart. Just go with me on this.
Farewell, John Bogle John Bogle, the founder of Vanguard and one of the greatest and most influential investors of all time, passed away Wednesday . His great contribution was to popularize buy-and-hold indexing with a focus on controlling costs. Using this approach, Bogle created unfathomable incremental wealth for investors large and small.
The elegant simplicity of Bogle's strategy - on average, no one beats the market, so just focus on costs - belies its revolutionary nature. Bogle upended the investment industry's lucrative management fee schedule, transferring wealth from Wall Street's bottom line into Main Street retirement accounts. The audacity of his vision is partially obscured today by the simple fact that his approach is now the default. (Look no further than Vanguard's appearance in " The Stupid Idiot's Guide To Investing Your Little Bit Of Money " to understand the extent of Bogle's influence.) His "set-and-forget" approach is also the unseen root system from which entire forest of quantitative management and systematic factor-based investing has grown. It's no overstatement to say his solutions to investing's behavioral economics problems rival those of Nobel prize winners like Richard Thaler or Daniel Kahneman.
As it happens, Bogle also had a tremendous indirect influence on me. I took an MBA internship at Vanguard's communications and marketing department in the summer of 2012. Today I remain struck by the company's tremendously powerful culture: Cost consciousness, prudence, focus on the long term. The investors - Vanguard's owner-customers - are the unending focus. Bogle's commitment to the steady, boring process of responsible wealth generation permeates every activity on the unassuming Malvern, PA, campus.
My bosses even ate like Vanguard employees. They took me to Wegman's for lunch my first day, and we went to a local sub shop for lunch on my last day. The sandwich is a total Vanguard food: straightforward ingredients, simple implementation, reliable results. Thrifty.
I've taken away from my brief time in Bogle's long shadow a clear idea of what business leadership is: Relentless commitment to core principles. Amid today's tech monopoly controversies and a persistent hum of financial market shenanigans, this is worth dwelling on: Vanguard doesn't have a culture problem. Everyone knows to put the investor first, and how to do it.
Not that proper execution is easy. My mentor at Vanguard told me the biggest difficulty of his communications role was, "It becomes very difficult to get people's attention when you're saying the same thing over and over again." It's also hard to fight human nature. Vanguard's investors are no different from anyone else. They get in their own way. They want to buy when stocks have gone up, they want to sell after crashes. When combating emotional preferences and deep-rooted psychological bias, most asset managers lose. Bogle found a way to win, through charisma, culture, and constant repetition of sound principles. People underestimate how hard it is to stick to a strategy that's easy to articulate and boring to implement. Bogle pulled it off.
In remembering Bogle's elegant achievements, we risk forgetting his genius as an investment analyst, his ability to navigate complexity. I'll take one representative passage on tax deferral from Common Sense on Mutual Funds.
The serious problem created by the relatively prompt realizations of capital gains by funds is that investors must pay taxes on them almost immediately. Yet the truly enormous value of deferring capital gains taxes seems almost universally ignored. To put it simply: A tax that is deferred is the functional equivalent of an interest-free loan from the U.S. Treasury Department, with a maturity equal to the number of years of deferral. You will probably owe the tax someday, but you don't have to pay it until then. Just imagine the value of a 10-year interest-free loan, or even a 25-year loan. Better still, calculate it. A $1.00 loan repayment deferred for 10 years has a present value of 47 cents; with a 25 year loan, that figure is just 15 cents! But mutual fund history suggests that as few as 5 percent of all fund holdings can be expected to be held for 10 years, and thus gain that 53 cent bonus on each dollar deferred for a decade, to say nothing of the bonus of 85 cents per dollar over a quarter century.
Ultimately, Bogle's towering influence and Vanguard's corporate culture failed to conquer my own human desire for excitement, risk, and quick results. This was obvious to everyone by the end of my summer in Malvern, and I wasn't asked to join Vanguard full time when my internship ended. "You would've loved it here in the 1980s," one veteran told me. "We were the insurgents." That line is partly what eventually led me to Seeking Alpha, which in its better moments shares elements of Vanguard's mission to help and inform investors.
Even though I didn't stick as a career Vanguard man, I'm more or less a Bogle style investor. While I love security analysis and actively manage a portion of my portfolio, the majority of my wealth is in passive funds. Much of how I think about corporate strategy and ethics also comes from my brief time there. Today, when our most disruptive and influential companies treat their stakeholders with unsettling ambivalence, we're well served to draw inspiration from John Bogle, whose contribution to the joint worlds of investing and entrepreneurship will hopefully never fade.

Jack Bogle Made Investors Money (Podcast) Should You Ignore John C. Bogle? Invest Like Dalio Or Like Bogle? Passive Wins (For Now) Jack Bogle Was Right - You Could Be Leaving 80% On The Table PG&E And Existential Falling Knives Over the years I've looked at corporate scandals and missteps as potential buying opportunities. Dilbert cartoonist Scott Adams has a very user-friendly (if a bit unsavory) description of this strategy in this Wall Street Journal article about betting " on the bad guys ."
I most recently thought of this strategy when PG&E ( PCG ) started cratering in early-mid November. The stock market can overreact to bad news, partly because initial guesses about regulatory punishment can be too pessimistic, but also because some investors seem to say "Yuck, the heck with this!" and simply sell.
PCG data by YCharts
My most recent and salient memory of this is the Volkswagen emissions scandal ( OTCPK:VLKAF ). I considered going long in October 2015 as the crisis unfolded, but never pulled the trigger.
VLKAF data by YCharts
What's interesting to me is that on a superficial price to sales and price to book value basis*, October 2015 gave Volkswagen investors the most attractive valuation of any time in the past five years. But I'm not persuaded that diving in would've been a great idea. The stock did outpace the S&P 500 for the next three years, but I can't think of a reason I would've sold at a good time, and since then shares have fallen back to pace with the broad index. My conclusion won't shock you: Investors shouldn't expect to bat 1.000 by bargain shopping when horrendous news hits a stock.
So back to PG&E. The stock is down around 85% since the wildfire news started coming out. The news coverage since November has been an evolving trainwreck, including plenty of sell-side upgrades and endorsements of the company. A few quick traders might have caught part of the 40%-ish countertrend rally in November, but mostly this has been a disaster. We definitely have a Dilbert situation here.
Among recent Seeking Alpha authors to weigh in is Robert Howard, CFA, whose December utilities review rightly features PG&E as the main attraction. Here's his summary.
The overhang of the wildfires from the last two years continued to plague the stock, but December brought more bad news. On the 14th the CPUC announced an investigation into PCG's gas business to see if they have been falsifying records and violating safety standards. (See article here .) A week later the CPUC discussed its investigation of PCG's culture, and whether the company should bring in new leadership, if it should divide itself into smaller companies, or if it should become a publicly owned utility. These negative stories continued to pound on the stock and led to its terrible performance.
Since then PG&E has announced plans to file for bankruptcy and missed an interest payment . As difficulties mount, it's actually kind of amazing the market was pricing in $3.3 billion in equity value as of Friday afternoon. It's bad, man. Robert Howard did a nice job gaming out the bankruptcy scenario:
For the bonds, the range of potential outcomes is narrower. If bankruptcy was declared the bonds could potentially take a haircut but that would mean wiping out the approximately $10B of current equity value, the $1.4B of wildfire insurance coverage , and the $3B+ of cash the company has on hand. Additionally, bankruptcy means that the solutions California devises to keep a utility running in northern California are not enough to meet PCG's normal obligations. This is not impossible, but it seems unlikely. So in a few years after these issues are resolved the bonds would likely start trading much closer to par.
More recently, SA author Khen Elazar has offered lessons from the PG&E experience for dividend growth investors, who often consider utility companies as safe and steady investments. For him, having a plan for adverse events is paramount.
My selling strategy is to sell when a company fails to achieve the goals, I set for it. As a dividend growth investor, I expect a company to pay me growing stream of dividends. I can deal with a dividend being frozen for a while, but a dividend cut will result in immediate sell. [...] Selling [PG&E] for $40 after the dividend cut could preserve some capital, and even before the declaration of bankruptcy, the share price lagged. The same capital could have achieved higher returns elsewhere.
Elazar also references the importance of diversification and the danger of projecting past dividend track records into the future. "The longest streak in history means nothing when a big blow hits a company," he says.
Elazar is bearish on PG&E, and no other articles have written it up since the bankruptcy announcement. I checked share borrow availability at Interactive Brokers and saw 2.6 million shares available Friday afternoon. Is the upside case a Volkswagen analog, where the stock muddles along in step with the S&P 500? Or is this a zero? I don't have the stones for this one, but I'll be watching.
*I understand the argument to use enterprise value metrics for companies with big balance sheets and bankruptcy concerns; just doing some illustrative first-order thinking here.

You might want to quote the author, who justly points out that 'investors must feel safe enough to stay with the strategy even if equities decline by 20% to 50%, which they might well do during a bear market.'"
Kevin Wilson explores the factors contributing to and coinciding with recessions . "A global recession appears to have already started, but there is also risk of another financial crisis," he says. You don't need to agree with his conclusions to find value in the numerous charts and pieces of historical context he brings to his analysis.
